If someone feels "hard done by," they feel that they have been treated unfairly or harshly — by a person, a situation, or life in general. They believe they deserve better than what they have received.

Think of it simply as: "I was treated badly, and it wasn't fair."

To truly understand an idiom, it helps to look at its individual words.

"Hard" — In everyday modern English, "hard" usually means "difficult." But in this idiom, "hard" is used in an older sense, meaning harshly or severely. This older usage still survives in phrases like "hard words" (cruel words) or "hitting someone hard."

"Done by" — This means treated or dealt with. Think of the famous moral principle: "Do unto others as you would have them do unto you." "Done by" works the same way — it means the way someone has been dealt with.

So, put together, "hard done by" literally means "treated harshly" or "dealt with severely."
The Key Nuance — Is the Feeling Justified?

This is the most important subtlety of this idiom, and most learners miss it.

When someone says they feel "hard done by," it does not automatically mean they were actually treated unfairly. The phrase describes how a person feels, not necessarily what truly happened.

This means the phrase can be used in two ways:

When the complaint is genuine and fair:
A worker who was fired without reason and without pay truly was treated unjustly. If she says she feels hard done by, she is right, and the listener would agree with her.

When the complaint seems exaggerated or self-pitying:
A teenager who wasn't allowed to go to a party and sulks and says he feels "hard done by" may be overreacting. In this case, the person saying it to describe him might be gently mocking his self-pity.

So depending on the context, the phrase can express genuine sympathy for unfair treatment or a mild, slightly amused criticism of someone who is complaining too much. A good learner always looks at the surrounding context to figure out which meaning is intended.

This is a piece of British English that has been in use for centuries. It grew out of older grammatical structures in the English language, where "done by" simply meant "treated." Over time, the combination of "hard" (harshly) + "done by" (treated) became a fixed expression.

Today, it is very common in British, Australian, Irish, and other Commonwealth varieties of English. If you are learning American English, be aware that Americans rarely use this phrase and may not immediately recognise it. It is not "wrong" in American English — it is simply uncommon there.
Grammar — How to Use It Correctly

"Hard done by" is almost always used as a predicative adjective — meaning it comes after a verb, not directly before a noun.

The most common patterns are:

feel hard done by — She felt hard done by after being left out.

be hard done by — He was hard done by in that deal.

seem hard done by — The team seemed hard done by after the referee's decision.

You can also hyphenate it when using it before a noun in informal writing: "a hard-done-by employee" — but this usage is less common. Stick to using it after verbs like feel, be, seem, look and you will almost never go wrong.

These examples show the phrase in a variety of real-life situations, so you can feel its range:

"After working overtime for months without a pay rise, she felt completely hard done by."
→ Her frustration is understandable and likely justified.

"He's always feeling hard done by, even when things are going perfectly well for him."
→ Here, the speaker is gently criticising someone for being unnecessarily self-pitying.

"The losing team felt hard done by after the match was decided by a controversial penalty."
→ The players feel they were treated unfairly by the referee's decision.

"Growing up the youngest of five children, she always felt hard done by when it came to getting new clothes."
→ A personal feeling from childhood, which may or may not have been truly unfair.

"Don't feel hard done by — everyone faces setbacks at some point."
→ Someone is telling another person not to wallow in self-pity.

The phrase often carries a slightly weary or resigned emotional tone. It is not explosive anger — it is more of a quiet, simmering sense of injustice. Think of someone sighing and saying "It just wasn't fair" rather than someone shouting in rage.

When used to describe another person (rather than expressing your own feeling), it can carry a tone of gentle mockery or mild exasperation, as if to say "there they go again, thinking the world is against them."

Knowing related expressions helps you understand the full picture:

"Get a raw deal" — to receive unfair treatment, especially in a transaction or arrangement. She got a raw deal when her partner took all the credit for her work.

"Short-changed" — to receive less than what you deserve. The workers felt short-changed by the new contract.

"Treated unfairly" — a plain, direct equivalent, though less idiomatic.

"Put upon" — to feel that others are taking advantage of you and loading too much onto you. She always felt put upon because she was the only one doing the housework.

All of these share the feeling of being on the receiving end of something unjust, but "hard done by" is broader and more general — it covers any kind of harsh or unfair treatment.

"Hard done by" means feeling that you have been treated unfairly or harshly. It comes from British English and is widely used across Commonwealth countries. It describes a feeling — which may or may not be fully justified. It almost always follows verbs like feel, be, or seem. Depending on context, it can express genuine sympathy or a subtle suggestion that someone is being a little too self-pitying.

If you remember nothing else, remember this sentence:
"She felt hard done by" = "She felt she had been treated unfairly."
